title: What the teams said – Thursday in Azerbaijan
excerpt:
The drivers and teams report back on all the action from Thursday practice in Baku ahead of the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

Sep 24, 2026 6:25pm UTC

Mercedes

Antonelli’s weekend started well when he went quickest on the hard tyre at the start of FP1, but it soon derailed as the youngster parked up with a hydraulics issue. Russell wound up on top of the opening session, despite running wide on his first push lap with conditions particularly testing for the drivers out there. Russell backed up that performance with a series of quick laps in FP2, once again winding up on top of the standings. Antonelli missed a chunk of running thanks to a PU change between sessions, but once he came out he was also quick and backed his team mate up with a second place finish, setting up a tasty intra-team battle for tomorrow.

Kimi Antonelli - FP1: 1:46.265, P5; FP2: 1:43.899, P2

"It was a somewhat compromised day due to the hydraulics issue we encountered, which cost us a significant amount of track time across both FP1 and FP2. We’re still working to understand exactly what caused the problem, but the team did a great job investigating it and, as a precaution, we changed the power unit to get back on track and complete some valuable running.

"Despite the disruption, I felt comfortable in the car from the laps we were able to complete. We focused on maximising every opportunity and recovering as much track time as possible. Losing laps is never ideal, particularly on a street circuit like Baku where confidence builds with every run, but ending the day in P2 was a positive way to recover. The car felt good throughout, and we’ll keep working hard to build on that as the weekend progresses."

George Russell - FP1: 1:45.387, P1; FP2: 1:43.347, P1

"It’s been a positive first day here in Baku. The car felt competitive over a single lap, and our race pace looks closely matched with McLaren and Red Bull. I’m sure those gaps will tighten even further when we get to qualifying tomorrow, so there’s still plenty of work to do overnight. Overall, though, it’s been an encouraging start to the weekend and a strong opening day for the team."

Andrew Shovlin, Trackside Engineering Director

"We've had a solid day overall. George's car ran reliably throughout; he topped both sessions and completed a productive long run. There are still areas we can improve, as is always the case on a Friday, but the car is behaving well, and we're encouraged by what we've seen so far. We don't expect the gaps on today's timesheets to be representative of the true competitive picture. Several of our competitors left time on the table during their soft tyre runs, so we know the field is likely much closer than it appears.

"Kimi's day was more disrupted. A hydraulic leak on his second run in FP1 brought an early end to the session after just three push laps. As a precaution, we elected to change the power unit, which delayed the start of his FP2 and cost him further running. Despite that, he was able to complete a useful mix of low and high-fuel work, and his pace was encouraging given the limited track time he had available. There is plenty to analyse overnight and some small gains to find, but overall we've made a positive start to the weekend."

BAKU, AZERBAIJAN - SEPTEMBER 24: George Russell of Great Britain driving the (63) Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team W17 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Azerbaijan at Baku City Circuit on September 24, 2026 in Baku, Azerbaijan. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

BAKU, AZERBAIJAN - SEPTEMBER 24: Andrea Kimi Antonelli of Italy driving the (12) Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team W17 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Azerbaijan at Baku City Circuit on September 24, 2026 in Baku, Azerbaijan. (Photo by Mark Thompson/Getty Images)

Red Bull

Verstappen and Hadjar both complained about their brakes early doors, but the Dutchman’s issues seemed to settle down, and he managed plenty of laps from there. Hadjar did not – he was told to coast back to the pits with what sounded like a PU problem, and he did not return to the track. That was a blow for the Frenchman, who is in desperate need of laps.

The good news is after a gearbox change between the sessions, Hadjar was able to get plenty of laps under his belt in the second session. And the even better news is the car looked quick, with Verstappen winding up in the top three in both sessions despite a few more varied complaints about his RB22.

Max Verstappen - FP1: 1:45.787, P2; FP2: 1:44.174, P3

“Today was quite decent and I was pretty happy with the car. We were working on fine-tuning a few bits and trying to find some more performance, so it was a good start for the Team. It looks like we are up there at the moment and could be fighting for a podium place, so we just need to find a bit more pace. The upgrades are working well, which is positive, so we will see how it plays out tomorrow.”

Isack Hadjar - FP1: 1:47.873, P20; FP2: 1:44.868, P9

"It's been a good return for me today. With the gearbox issue I was only able to get a few laps in, but I was really happy with the feeling of the car and enjoyed being back out there. In both FP1 and FP2 I didn't manage to get many push laps, so it's hard to judge the true one-lap pace, but we still have tomorrow to do that. With the upgrades the characteristics of the car are the same, but it feels stronger than what I drove in Budapest, and I think we're in the mix with McLaren and Ferrari. I'm excited to go again tomorrow."

Pierre Wache, Technical Director

"Overall, it was quite a positive day from the start of FP1 onwards, apart from the gearbox problem we had on Isack's car, which we managed to fix in time for FP2. We received good feedback from both drivers about the balance of the car and the upgrades we brought. There are some things we need to fix, and we are looking to find some more speed until tomorrow. Mercedes looks like the fastest car, especially on the short runs, McLaren and Ferrari are hard to assess due to a lot happening on track, but we should be up there with them. It was good to see Isack back in the car and being competitive and up to speed straight away, with no issues concerning his wrist."

BAKU, AZERBAIJAN - SEPTEMBER 24: Max Verstappen of the Netherlands driving the (3) Oracle Red Bull Racing RB22 Red Bull Ford Powertrains on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Azerbaijan at Baku City Circuit on September 24, 2026 in Baku, Azerbaijan. (Photo by Ryan Pierse/Getty Images)

BAKU, AZERBAIJAN - SEPTEMBER 24: Isack Hadjar of France and Oracle Red Bull Racing prepares to drive in the garage during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Azerbaijan at Baku City Circuit on September 24, 2026 in Baku, Azerbaijan. (Photo by Mark Thompson/Getty Images)

Ferrari

Ferrari opted not to run the soft tyres in FP1, with both drivers managing clean sessions. Leclerc was the faster of the two by just 0.033s, as the team experimented with the tow at times. It was much of the same in FP2, both looking quick and relatively well matched. On a day where the other big teams all had issues, Ferrari had by far the most straightforward of days. But they do need to find some pace if they want to challenge Mercedes tomorrow.

Charles Leclerc - FP1: 1:45.791, P3; FP2: 1:44.473, P4

"We lacked some pace in the practice sessions so there is quite a lot of work to do tonight to close the gap. We will go through everything we learned today and work on making a step forward ahead of tomorrow. Hopefully we can come back stronger for qualifying on a track that I really enjoy driving."

Lewis Hamilton - FP1: 1:45.824, P4; FP2: 1:44.665, P5

"It is always great to drive at this circuit and it’s been a productive day overall. FP1 was encouraging and we completed a number of consistent laps and established a useful baseline to build from. There are a few areas we need to examine more closely, but we have gathered a considerable amount of data and will use tonight to understand where we can make further progress.

"Tyre preparation remains an important focus, particularly in ensuring we can consistently bring them into the right operating window. That has a significant impact on both available grip and the overall balance of the car, so it will be a key priority as we prepare for tomorrow."

BAKU, AZERBAIJAN - SEPTEMBER 24: Charles Leclerc of Monaco driving the (16) Scuderia Ferrari SF-26 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Azerbaijan at Baku City Circuit on September 24, 2026 in Baku, Azerbaijan. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

BAKU, AZERBAIJAN - SEPTEMBER 24: Lewis Hamilton of Great Britain driving the (44) Scuderia Ferrari SF-26 leaves the garage during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Azerbaijan at Baku City Circuit on September 24, 2026 in Baku, Azerbaijan. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

McLaren

McLaren had a messy first session in Baku, with both drivers spending time in the garage. Piastri complained about his brakes early on before being brought in twice more to check for damage to the car, while Norris did not get many laps in due to some loose bodywork. The team seemed to still be running some interesting fixes to the cars in FP2, with cable ties in evidence, but the good news is both drivers got plenty of laps. Neither wound up right at the sharp end of the top 10, but the team have time overnight to implement some more permanent fixes to their bodywork issues.

Lando Norris - FP1: 1:46.981, P14; FP2: 1:44.831, P6

“A tricky start today after losing some laps in FP1 which wasn’t ideal, but the team in the garage did a solid job to get the cars ready for FP2 and that’s a positive we’ll carry forward. Overall, the car actually feels pretty good to drive, but on a slow-speed track with a long straight we’re losing out and being off the pace is a tough start. We’ll now dig into the data overnight and see what we can change for tomorrow’s sessions, I hope we can close some of the gap. We’ll keep our heads down and try to maximise what we have for the remainder of the weekend.”

Oscar Piastri - FP1: 1:46.398, P6; FP2: 1:44.857, P8

“An interesting but productive day. There’s lots to learn here with the new cars, and on a personal level it felt pretty positive overall. FP1 was a little disrupted with the reliability issue which meant we lost a bit of running, which is never ideal. But we’ve made some good steps in FP2, and we have some decent long run pace. The plan for tomorrow is to keep making steady improvements, unlock some more performance so that we can make up some of the gap to the Mercedes, and see what we can do in Qualifying.”

Rob Marshall, Chief Technical Officer & Chief Designer

“We've introduced a significant upgrade this weekend and the initial data suggests the car is behaving as our simulations predicted, which is a positive starting point. However, it's clear we haven't yet unlocked its full potential. The first session was slightly disrupted, and we are still in the process of dialling in both the chassis and the power unit to suit the unique demands of this circuit. We have a lot of data to analyse, but we are confident in our process.

“Our focus now is on the work we do overnight. We have a history of making strong progress from Free Practice into Qualifying, and that remains our objective. It's about building driver confidence, optimising the setup, and extracting the performance that we believe is in the package. There were no major shocks, and we are focused on the methodical work required to get us where we want to be for Qualifying.”

BAKU, AZERBAIJAN - SEPTEMBER 24: Lando Norris of Great Britain driving the (1) McLaren MCL40 Mercedes on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Azerbaijan at Baku City Circuit on September 24, 2026 in Baku, Azerbaijan. (Photo by Adam Pretty/Getty Images)

BAKU, AZERBAIJAN - SEPTEMBER 24: Oscar Piastri of Australia driving the (81) McLaren MCL40 Mercedes on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Azerbaijan at Baku City Circuit on September 24, 2026 in Baku, Azerbaijan. (Photo by Mark Thompson/Getty Images)

Racing Bulls

Lawson looked like he had never left Racing Bulls, the New Zealander having a clean first session. He wound up solidly in the top 10 along with his team mate, although Lindblad had one moment where he wound up down in one of the run off areas. He took a while to get going, but was able to continue under his own steam. But the rookie’s luck did not hold in FP2, Lindblad the first to properly find the walls. He fell foul of the Turn 8-9-10 complex, hitting the wall twice and bringing out the red flags after just four laps.

That leaves him very short of running heading into Friday, while Lawson fell down the order in FP2 and thus needs to find some time to try and compete for Q3 tomorrow.

Arvid Lindblad - FP1: 1:46.601, P8; FP2: 1:46.391, P18

“It wasn’t the best day for us today. I apologise to the team for the crash in FP2; it's a shame, as overall I felt pretty good in the car. We’ll look at everything tonight and see where we can improve and make a few changes ahead of tomorrow. My main focus now is to get back into the rhythm and bounce back for the rest of the weekend. Maximising FP3 will be really important to put ourselves in the best possible position heading into Qualifying.”

Liam Lawson - FP1: 1:46.440, P7; FP2: 1:45.681, P12

“It was nice to be back in my own car today. The morning was pretty positive and we were feeling competitive, but the other teams seemed to make a step forward in FP2, so we’ll look into that and try to make another step ourselves for tomorrow. Overall, it’ been a good day and it’s great to be back home. It’s going to be very close this weekend, so I’m looking forward to Qualifying around here. ”

Alan Permane, Team Principal

“It’s been a pretty decent day today overall. We’re where we thought we would be and have some time to make some changes ahead of tomorrow. It was a bit of a shame for Arvid, he was pushing hard and just went a bit too far, but the car was feeling good up until then and he was significantly up on the lap, which was positive.

“It’s great to have Liam back in the car. Arvid and Liam work very well together and their joint feedback improves both cars through the weekend. From what we’ve seen today, our target remains both cars in Q3 tomorrow.”

BAKU, AZERBAIJAN - SEPTEMBER 24: Arvid Lindblad of Great Britain and Visa Cash App Racing Bulls gets out of the car after hitting the wall during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Azerbaijan at Baku City Circuit on September 24, 2026 in Baku, Azerbaijan. (Photo by Adam Pretty/Getty Images)

BAKU, AZERBAIJAN - SEPTEMBER 24: Arvid Lindblad of Great Britain driving the (41) Visa Cash App Racing Bulls VCARB 03 RB Ford hits the wall during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Azerbaijan at Baku City Circuit on September 24, 2026 in Baku, Azerbaijan. (Photo by Mark Thompson/Getty Images)

BAKU, AZERBAIJAN - SEPTEMBER 24: Liam Lawson of New Zealand and Visa Cash App Racing Bulls prepares to drive in the garage during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Azerbaijan at Baku City Circuit on September 24, 2026 in Baku, Azerbaijan. (Photo by Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images)

Alpine

Alpine were one of very few teams to have a quiet opening session, with no obvious issues. They wound up down the order, building slowly into their weekend. Alpine did split strategies in FP1, Colapinto running the mediums and Gasly the hards. Those two swapped around in FP2, Gasly on the mediums as Colapinto ran the hard tyre. The Argentine had one odd moment, using the run off area at Turn 1 despite not locking up, seemingly forgetting to steer for the corner. But aside from that, they jumped a few spots up the leaderboard, with Gasly slotting nicely into the top 10.

Pierre Gasly - FP1: 1:47.043, P16; FP2: 1:44.843, P7

“It's been a good day in the car, especially Free Practice 2 where we ended up in P7 on the leaderboard. I think we can be pleased as a team with today, where I have generally felt good in the car. It is always tricky in Baku with the conditions and it's a track where you never feel totally comfortable. I was pushing the limits more and more on each lap so it's positive to build up an idea of what the car can do. Right now, I am happy with our work and I am feeling good going into the rest of the weekend. We saw some of our rivals in the midfield bring upgrades, which I am sure will help them unlock more performance. We'll focus on ourselves, though, and our aim is to keep the form going after our positive day.”

Franco Colapinto - FP1: 1:47.523, P18; FP2: 1:45.479, P11

“We had a challenging but productive first day here in Baku and we ended in a much more positive position compared to where we started. The track was quite dirty and low grip in Free Practice 1 and there was a lot of track evolution as the day went on, as is expected on street circuits. The session was quite interrupted with yellow flags, which impacted our running, but we knew there was more pace in the car to unlock. We then made a step heading into Free Practice 2 and that was a better session for us which I think reflected our pace a bit more. We still have lots to improve with the car and will work hard as a team tonight to try and make more progress as we aim for another positive Qualifying tomorrow.”

Steve Nielsen, Managing Director

“We did plenty of work today and, on a track of this nature, the more laps you do the more you can learn as the grip increases and the drivers grow in confidence. It's always been a difficult track to get right, especially early in the weekend with the conditions and lack of grip throughout the lap. We made good progress in Free Practice 2 once both Pierre and Franco had some clean, consistent laps. In the end, that session proved more reflective of the pace in our car with Pierre in P7 and Franco knocking on the door of the top ten, which obviously bodes well. There is potential there, certainly a little more performance to find, and the aim, as always every weekend, is to have both drivers compete for Q3 and be in contention to score points."

BAKU, AZERBAIJAN - SEPTEMBER 24: Pierre Gasly of France driving the (10) Alpine F1 A526 Mercedes on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Azerbaijan at Baku City Circuit on September 24, 2026 in Baku, Azerbaijan. (Photo by Bryn Lennon - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

BAKU, AZERBAIJAN - SEPTEMBER 24: Franco Colapinto of Argentina driving the (43) Alpine F1 A526 Mercedes on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Azerbaijan at Baku City Circuit on September 24, 2026 in Baku, Azerbaijan. (Photo by Ryan Pierse/Getty Images)

Haas

Ocon looked quick in FP1, finishing in the top 10 but he did have one hairy moment when his car stopped at the pit lane exit. He managed eventually to get going, which was good news as he was able to then finish the session and complete a practice start. In FP2 it was Bearman’s turn to fall foul of reliability, as he had an engine issue down the straight and parked straight up at the back of the run off area. He spent the rest of FP2 watching the action from a marshal’s chair, while Ocon made it back-to-back sessions in the top 10.

Esteban Ocon – FP1: 1:46.624, P9; FP2: 1:45.290, P10

“I think the pace of the car is pretty decent – we found a good rhythm out there, improving lap by lap. From FP1, the first lap I completed, I was P6 or P7, so I thought we could work from there. We had a decent feel and the car feels healthy, so hopefully it can continue for the rest of the weekend. It was a much nicer day than last year where I couldn’t brake anywhere – now we can attack the corners, which is very nice.”

Oliver Bearman - FP1: 1:46.994, P15; FP2: 1:46.801, P20

“It was a tough day with a failure on the car, which meant I didn’t really get any laps in FP2. Generally though, it felt like a better afternoon than morning, so we made a step forward on the car, and I’m quite happy about that. We’ll see what we can do tomorrow, as it’s tough missing out on both low- and high-fuel running, but I had good confidence, so we’ll do our best for Friday.”

Ayao Komatsu, Team Principal

“It was a mixed day really because it wasn’t a trouble-free FP1, and in FP2, Ollie had another PU issue which ended his session – so we’re still investigating the cause of that, as that’s concerning. A bit like Madrid, the tyres are on the edge, but when you get tyre preparation right, it seems like our car has speed. Car balance is pretty good and it gives our drivers confidence, which is exactly what you need at a street circuit like this. There are positive signs in terms of car performance, but we need to get to the bottom of this reliability issue and then tomorrow morning, focus on quali tyre preparation. If we execute well, I believe we can fight.”

BAKU, AZERBAIJAN - SEPTEMBER 24: Esteban Ocon of France driving the (31) Haas F1 VF-26 Ferrari on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Azerbaijan at Baku City Circuit on September 24, 2026 in Baku, Azerbaijan. (Photo by Peter Fox/Getty Images)

BAKU, AZERBAIJAN - SEPTEMBER 24: Oliver Bearman of Great Britain driving the (87) Haas F1 VF-26 Ferrari on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Azerbaijan at Baku City Circuit on September 24, 2026 in Baku, Azerbaijan. (Photo by Bryn Lennon - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Audi

Audi are running an extensive upgrade package here, and used FP1 to gather plenty of data using aero rakes and flow-vis paint. They were also the team to most obviously experiment with the tow down the main straight. Hulkenberg’s session did not end in ideal fashion, as he parked up late on and helped the marshals push his car away. Both drivers faded in the second session, but with the red flag interruptions, it is hard to say how much pace they have in hand heading into tomorrow.

Nico Hulkenberg - FP1: 1:46.871, P11; FP2: 1:45.854, P15

“Overall, it was a reasonable Friday. I ran the previous specification in FP1 before switching to the new parts for FP2, so there was plenty of information to gather and a lot for us to understand. The sessions were not entirely straightforward, with a few challenges to work through, but the underlying picture is encouraging. Now it’s about going through everything overnight, cleaning up a few areas and seeing how we can put it all together tomorrow. If we do that, I think we can be competitive.”

Gabriel Bortoleto - FP1: 1:46.688, P10; FP2: 1:45.794, P14

“It’s been a bit of a test day for us with the new package, and we have plenty of data to analyse to get the general picture of it. We are lacking a little bit of grip at the moment, but Baku is a low-grip and very dusty circuit, so we have some work to do to put everything in place. Let’s see what we can do tomorrow from here.”

BAKU, AZERBAIJAN - SEPTEMBER 24: Nico Hulkenberg of Germany driving the (27) Audi F1 Team R26 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Azerbaijan at Baku City Circuit on September 24, 2026 in Baku, Azerbaijan. (Photo by Bryn Lennon - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

BAKU, AZERBAIJAN - SEPTEMBER 24: Gabriel Bortoleto of Brazil driving the (5) Audi F1 Team R26 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Azerbaijan at Baku City Circuit on September 24, 2026 in Baku, Azerbaijan. (Photo by Mark Thompson/Getty Images)

Williams

Williams did not have the dream start to their weekend when Sainz’s brakes caught fire early on, a radio issue meaning he could not tell the team he was coming in. The damage was not extensive, so he did not miss too much running. Which was just as well as they looked quick, that new chassis doing the business and jumping them closer to the top 10. Both drivers went backwards down the order in FP2, but with plenty learned about their new chassis, they will be hopeful of finding some time overnight once the data is analysed.

Alex Albon - FP1: 1:46.939, P13; FP2: 1:46.123, P16

"That’s Friday finished with our main talking points focusing on the upgrades. I think we've shown that we're a little bit more competitive and the cars are behaving pretty well, but there’s still some things to learn and improve on. We'll look at the data tonight to assess how we can improve the balance for both of us heading into tomorrow."

Carlos Sainz - FP1: 1:46.893, P12; FP2: 1:46.391, P17

"Today felt like a step forward as we expected - there were no massive surprises. Unfortunately we had quite a scrappy day with a lack of running in FP1 and FP2 because of some issues with the car, including the brakes. So we didn't get all the laps in to evaluate everything that we would have liked, but we still have FP3 to do it. In general I feel a bit better with the car and it seems like we’re a bit closer to the midfield. I feel like I'm in a good place and now we need to make the right steps going into tomorrow."

BAKU, AZERBAIJAN - SEPTEMBER 24: Carlos Sainz of Spain driving the (55) Williams FW48 Mercedes in the Pitlane during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Azerbaijan at Baku City Circuit on September 24, 2026 in Baku, Azerbaijan. (Photo by Ryan Pierse/Getty Images)

BAKU, AZERBAIJAN - SEPTEMBER 24: Alexander Albon of Thailand driving the (23) Williams FW48 Mercedes on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Azerbaijan at Baku City Circuit on September 24, 2026 in Baku, Azerbaijan. (Photo by Mark Thompson/Getty Images)

Cadillac

On a day where overheating brakes were an issue, Cadillac’s fix to their own brake problems seemed to be working, with both drivers able to manage a good haul of laps in FP1. Perez wound up an impressive P17, showing their pace from Madrid was not an anomaly. The Mexican did even better in FP2, finishing up in 13th which bodes well for the team as they fight for a first Q2 appearance of the season.

Valtteri Bottas - FP1: 1:49.315, P22; FP2: 1:46.737, P19

Sergio Perez - FP1: 1:47.253, P17; FP2: 1:45.760, P13

BAKU, AZERBAIJAN - SEPTEMBER 24: Sergio Perez of Mexico driving the (11) Cadillac F1 Team MAC-26 Ferrari on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Azerbaijan at Baku City Circuit on September 24, 2026 in Baku, Azerbaijan. (Photo by Adam Pretty/Getty Images)

BAKU, AZERBAIJAN - SEPTEMBER 24: Valtteri Bottas of Finland driving the (77) Cadillac F1 Team MAC-26 Ferrari on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Azerbaijan at Baku City Circuit on September 24, 2026 in Baku, Azerbaijan. (Photo by Peter Fox/Getty Images)

Aston Martin

Aston Martin had a steady opening session, both drivers managing plenty of laps. News soon broke that both Alonso and Stroll have grid penalties to come for the Grand Prix, after taking on new power unit components. As such, they used up some soft tyres in FP2, but Alonso spent much of the session back in the garage as the team investigated a suspected oil leak.

Fernando Alonso - FP1: 1:47.835, P19; FP2: 1:47.889, P22

Lance Stroll - FP1: 1:48.547, P21; FP2: 1:47.403, P21

Stroll says:

"We got some laps in today and learned what we could, so we'll work on improving the car tonight and hopefully put ourselves in a better position tomorrow.

"We know we're struggling for pace, and with the penalties for the new power unit components, we'll be starting from the back of the grid. We'll focus on getting the most out of the weekend and hopefully putting ourselves in a position to take advantage of any opportunities that come our way."

Mike Krack, Chief Trackside Officer says:

"We can take some learnings from today's practice sessions, but we knew this would be a track that we would struggle at compared to our competitors.

"We agreed with Honda this weekend would be the better place to take some new components and so we took that decision. Fernando's car had a suspected oil leak halfway through FP2 which limited his running.

"We will check everything overnight and look to fix things in time for tomorrow's final practice session."

BAKU, AZERBAIJAN - SEPTEMBER 24: Fernando Alonso of Spain driving the (14) Aston Martin F1 Team AMR26 Honda Nico Hulkenberg of Germany driving the (27) Audi F1 Team R26 and Isack Hadjar of France driving the (6) Oracle Red Bull Racing RB22 Red Bull Ford Powertrains on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Azerbaijan at Baku City Circuit on September 24, 2026 in Baku, Azerbaijan. (Photo by Peter Fox/Getty Images)

BAKU, AZERBAIJAN - SEPTEMBER 24: Lance Stroll of Canada driving the (18) Aston Martin F1 Team AMR26 Honda on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Azerbaijan at Baku City Circuit on September 24, 2026 in Baku, Azerbaijan. (Photo by Bryn Lennon - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Pirelli

Simone Berra, Pirelli Chief Engineer

“It was a first day heavily influenced by a particularly dirty track, with dust even on the racing line, resulting in very significant track evolution. Lap times improved consistently throughout the day, with differences of up to two seconds between the two sessions. Compared to last year, the track surface appeared less favourable, particularly affecting the tyre warm-up phase.

"Teams focused their work on car set-up in order to bring the tyres into the correct operating window, especially on the front axle. This proved to be crucial both for maximising single-lap performance, which was often achieved only after several attempts, and for limiting the risk of braking lock-ups.

"The teams generally completed an intensive programme of work with all three compounds in preparation for a race that is increasingly expected to be a one-stop affair. Degradation levels were in fact very low, and track evolution almost completely offset tyre wear during some long runs, making lap times progressively quicker. We did not observe any graining, which is an interesting finding considering the very smooth track surface. In terms of lap time performance, the data indicates deltas broadly in line with simulations: around half a second between the C4 and C5, and a few tenths between the C3 and C4.

"Looking ahead to tomorrow, with lower temperatures and stronger wind gusts forecast, tyre preparation will once again be a key factor. The track will offer more grip than today, but teams will need to manage traffic and generate as much energy as possible in the tyres. For Saturday’s Grand Prix, all compounds remain theoretically viable, although the two softer options may take on a more prominent role in light of the expected drop in temperatures.”

title: Who are the favourites for the Haas seats in 2027?
excerpt:
Heading into the Azerbaijan Grand Prix weekend, Esteban Ocon identified himself as a “free agent” for the 2027 season, confirming that he’s yet to receive an offer of a contract extension at Haas. While his team mate Ollie Bearman hasn’t officially been announced as one of their drivers either, he seemed far more confident of keeping his seat – so who’s most likely to link up with the Briton next year?

Esteban Ocon

At 30 years old, Ocon has spent a third of his life competing in F1, which began in 2016 with stints at Manor and Force India before he took a sabbatical as a Mercedes reserve driver.

Speaking of the Silver Arrows, he became part of their junior team in 2015 and has maintained a link with the squad ever since – it was Team Principal Toto Wolff who gave him a shot in the top tier, and they still have a management relationship to an extent.

Ocon returned to a full-time seat with Renault – later rebranded as Alpine – and claimed both his maiden podium and victory at the 2020 Sakhir Grand Prix and 2021 Hungarian Grand Prix respectively.

Going up against the likes of Fernando Alonso and Pierre Gasly, the Frenchman was a consistent points finisher and contributed to Alpine’s strong position in the midfield, clinching additional podiums in Monaco and Sao Paulo.

'Definitely a free agent for next year’ – Ocon on Haas future

However, he was replaced by Jack Doohan for the 2024 season finale in Abu Dhabi and stated his departure was “not how I wanted things to end”, but was soon taken in by Haas on a multi-year deal beginning in 2025. That season, his rookie team mate Bearman marginally outscored him – a pattern which has continued into 2026, with Ocon on three points to the Briton’s 18.

For each Haas candidate, we asked F1 Correspondent & Presenter Lawrence Barretto for his take on how high their chances are.

Lawrence says: "While Ocon remains an option for Haas, sources suggest the Frenchman will part ways with the American squad when his deal expires at the end of this season. I understand his intention is to stay in Formula 1, but with opportunities on the 2027 grid limited, a reserve role is more likely."

Rafael Camara

Most of the grid’s 11 teams have announced unchanged driver line-ups for next season, so if we were to see a rookie make his debut, one of the most likely options would be Ferrari junior Rafael Camara.

The Brazilian’s childhood karting hobby soon transformed into a rapid rise through the ranks, and he stepped up to single-seaters as well as the Ferrari Driver Academy in 2022, joining current Haas driver Bearman in the Scuderia’s stable.

Top-three finishes in Formula 4 and Formula Regional followed before he progressed to Formula 3 for the 2025 season, winning the championship on his first attempt.

Who is Ferrari junior Rafael Camara?

That naturally progressed to a seat in Formula 2 where Camara has continued to impress – he currently sits P2 in the standings, just seven points behind another exciting talent in Nikola Tsolov.

His obvious skill and raw pace have earned him tests for both Ferrari and Haas, giving him the opportunity to drive their challengers from previous seasons and show just what he could do in an F1 car.

Lawrence says: "Camara is the overwhelming favourite to get the nod to take over Ocon's seat next year. The Ferrari junior impressed Haas when he got behind the wheel of one of their cars in the Test of Previous Cars (TPC) running while Ferrari, who have been a close partner of Haas since the team entered the sport in 2016, rate him highly and are very keen to test his potential in Formula 1."

Leonardo Fornaroli

Camara isn’t the only one who has taken part in a Testing of Previous Cars (TPC) day, with fellow young driver Leonardo Fornaroli having completed his own run earlier this year. But unlike the Brazilian, he didn’t have any tangible links to F1 teams for the bulk of his career.

Fornaroli did enjoy a similar progression through karting, F4 and Formula Regional, but spent an additional season in F3 and improved from P11 to P1 in the series over his two stints.

After clinching the title in 2024, he graduated to F2 and took four wins en route to adding another championship to his resume. Within days of his triumph, McLaren had signed the Italian to their development programme and handed him the role of reserve driver for 2026.

That opened the door for plenty of testing, including appearances in the MCL60 and an FP1 session in Barcelona, where he placed an eye-catching fifth. He then got the chance to drive Haas’ VF-25 in the aforementioned TPC day, providing the team with valuable data to compare him with their other 2027 candidates.

Lawrence says: "As Haas mulled their options regarding their 2027 line-up, Italian Fornaroli emerged as a strong contender. It's understood McLaren, who have signed him up to their development programme, were up for loaning him to Haas should they want him and it's believed he performed very strongly when running old-spec Haas machinery. But he has since dropped behind Camara on the shortlist."

Yuki Tsunoda

Yuki Tsunoda is no stranger to the F1 grid, having featured on it full-time for five seasons between 2021 and 2025. That partly came as a result of several years of backing from Honda, with their Formula Dream Project supporting him in his move from karting to junior formulae in 2016.

He then signed for the Red Bull Junior Team in 2019 and finished third in his rookie F2 season, receiving a promotion to their Honda-powered sister outfit AlphaTauri (now named Racing Bulls) for the 2021 campaign.

The Japanese racer’s speed was clear from the outset, but mistakes in his early seasons sometimes overshadowed his potential. As time went on, he held his own against team mates including Gasly, Daniel Ricciardo and Liam Lawson, eventually culminating in a shot alongside Max Verstappen at Red Bull.

Komatsu reveals timeline for Haas 2027 driver line-up decision

Unfortunately, his time at the top team saw him struggle to match the Dutchman – he achieved his best result of P5 in the 2025 Qatar Sprint and was replaced by Isack Hadjar at the end of the year, moving into a test and reserve role.

Staying in the Red Bull family paid off when he was called up to deputise Lawson this season, who in turn stepped in for an injured Hadjar for races in the Netherlands, Italy and Spain. Tsunoda proved that he hadn’t lost his driving ability as he scored at Monza, bringing him back into the limelight.

Lawrence says: "Tsunoda was part of the early conversation about drivers who Haas could potentially run in 2027 – and he put himself back in the shop window with a very assured super-sub performance across three races at Racing Bulls in place of the injured Hadjar. But the Honda-backed driver, who is one of the Red Bull family's reserves this year, doesn't appear to have enough traction to force himself into contention."

Ryo Hirakawa

Despite being neither an F2 graduate nor a former F1 driver, Ryo Hirakawa has been a consistent presence behind the scenes for several years.

He ascended through various series in his home country of Japan in his teenage years, becoming the youngest-ever champion in Japanese F3 before joining the Toyota Young Driver Program and moving to Super Formula and Super GT.

His sportscar experience was a fruitful one and led to him securing the 2017 Super GT title, but from 2022 onwards, Hirakawa switched his attention to the World Endurance Championship, sticking with Toyota throughout.

In his maiden season, he converted pole into victory at the prestigious 24 Hours of Le Mans alongside veteran racers Sebastien Buemi and Brendon Hartley, and went on to sign for McLaren as a reserve driver for 2024.

He’s participated in more FP1 sessions, when teams often choose to field rookies, than most – not just for McLaren, but also for Alpine and now Haas. His ties with Toyota aligned with the team's title partnership with Gazoo Racing, so he changed allegiance to the American outfit in 2025 and has regularly tested their cars over the last year or so.

Lawrence says: "Sources tell me Haas reserve and Toyota-backed driver Hirawaka has lapped very competitively every time he has got behind the wheel of a Haas, whether that's in a free practice session for young drivers on a Grand Prix weekend or a TPC test, but he is not expected to get the nod for promotion."

Jack Doohan

We briefly mentioned Doohan above as he took Ocon’s seat at Alpine for the final round of the 2024 season. He’s replaced the Frenchman before, so what’s to stop him doing it a second time?

The son of motorbike racing legend Mick Doohan, the Australian grew up around motorsport and began racing in a go-kart given to him by neighbour and family friend Michael Schumacher – not a bad way to start out.

Why Jack Doohan values childhood neighbour Michael Schumacher

That kickstarted a journey through F4 and F3, in which he settled for the runner-up position in his second full season. Doohan then improved to F2 and added more race wins to his tally, balancing the competition with a move from the Red Bull Junior Team to the Alpine Academy in 2022.

Like other junior drivers, he took part in test days and FP1 sessions to develop into a candidate for an F1 seat, which he was handed for a total of seven rounds before being replaced by Franco Colapinto.

His sudden demotion resulted in Doohan switching to Haas from the start of 2026, and he now acts as a reserve driver whilst taking on the European Le Mans Series.

Lawrence says: Doohan got himself a lifeline with Haas when he joined as a reserve driver for this year, having been let go by Alpine. The American team gave him some TPC running to evaluate him, but while he did a good job behind the wheel, he's not believed to be at the top of the shortlist.

title: Lawson returns as Lindblad hits trouble in Baku
excerpt:
It was an eventful Thursday for Racing Bulls in Azerbaijan as Liam Lawson settled back into life with the team after his Red Bull stint, while Arvid Lindblad faced the unforgiving challenge of Baku's streets.

The pair enjoyed a solid start to the weekend in FP1, finishing seventh and eighth respectively, but the second session told a different story.

While Lawson continued to build confidence behind the wheel, Lindblad's day ended early after a crash with the barriers brought out the red flags and left the team with work to do ahead of Friday.

The New Zealander went 12th fastest in FP2 but had a scary moment when the Ferrari of Lewis Hamilton suddenly appeared in front of him in the final sector while he was on a hot lap, meaning he had to take avoiding action.

Meanwhile, rookie driver Lindblad clouted the walls through the castle section 20 minutes into the session, bringing out the red flag and causing significant damage to the right-hand side of his car.

The British driver radioed his team to apologise, saying he'd just clipped the wall by a millimetre, having also crashed during FP2 in Madrid last time out.

Speaking after the session, Team Principal Alan Permane said he was not going to punish Lindblad for his mistake: "It’s not the time to come down on him like a ton of bricks, it’s the time to support him.

"It was a millimetre. It’s a bit of a shame. It’s certainly not the right time to crash like that, if that was Q3 and he was absolutely going for it, you can understand it. But it’s a little bit of 'the car was feeling good'. I think it’s just a little bit of rookie enthusiasm, but nothing more than that."

He added that Lindblad was looking quick on that lap and the team are going to take that as a positive going into the rest of the event.

Permane also welcomed the fact the squad have Lawson back after a three race stint covering Isack Hadjar at sister team Red Bull.

"Much as we love Yuki [Tsunoda] — and the whole team does, he’s a very popular figure – it’s good to have Liam back in his car, in the team, working very, very well with Arvid, and those two lift each other up through the weekend."

Lawson said himself afterwards that he was very happy to be back in his own car: "Honestly, it was good. This morning we were quite strong. We definitely didn’t have the same performance in FP2, where everybody else made a decent step, so we have to look at that and try and improve things for tomorrow.

"But overall, it’s good. It’s nice to be back in my car. It feels like home, but we have some work to do to match those guys."

The New Zealander added that the team will be working overnight to improve in the low speed corners to try and get themselves into the top 10 in Qualifying on Friday.

title: Audi's upgrade package 'delivering as expected' – Binotto
excerpt:
Audi Team Principal Mattia Binotto believes the team's major upgrade package, which has been introduced ahead of the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, is "delivering as expected".

The Hinwil outfit ticked 14 category boxes on the FIA’s pre-weekend submission list of aerodynamic upgrades, which includes substantially changed front and rear wings, a revised floor, and a new engine cover arrangement amongst others.

As part of the correlation process, only Gabriel Bortoleto had the updates in FP1, allowing for a direct comparison with Nico Hulkenberg’s older spec car in Baku.

“If you look at the first, let me say, impression of the data, the package is delivering as expected,” said Binotto.

“Which is good, which is our main focus, as a matter of fact, for the weekend. For us, upgrading, yes, it’s important for the performance, it’s important for our fight in the championship.

“But again, for us, what’s more important is to make sure that the team is developing in terms of methodologies and capacity.

"So from being brave when it comes to mindset, to the type of aero concepts we may deliver, on the lead times, engineering, production, manufacturing, we raised the challenge.

"With the upgrade we have brought here, it doesn’t matter how much it will deliver in terms of lap time.

"I think what matters for us the most is having raised the challenge, having again pushed the system on whatever is mindset and lead times, and hopefully we’ll have a correlation which is right compared to the wind tunnel and the sim.”

Audi sit eighth in the teams' standings, just four points behind Haas, with Hulkenberg and Bortoleto having finished in the points at five of the last six Grands Prix between them.

Bortoleto was able to finish P10 in FP1 with the new package, just ahead of Hulkenberg, before the pair finished P14 and P15 in the second session.

“I think the car didn't feel amazing in FP2,” said Bortoleto.

“If I'm very honest, we're lacking a little bit of grip, still to understand why. I don't have answers for that.

“I guess that's Baku, low grip, super dusty. The track has not been cleaned, I think, for a few years now, and yeah, just we need to drive with this and then try our best.”

title: 'Others just took another step' in Baku practice – Hamilton
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton believes "others just took another step" forward during Thursday practice ahead of the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, with Ferrari needing to find more performance if they are to challenge.

Hamilton and Ferrari team mate Charles Leclerc looked competitive during Free Practice 1 in Baku, the pair finishing third and fourth but only four tenths away from the top time having used the medium Pirelli tyre.

By the second session however, that margin had expanded to 1.1 seconds for Leclerc in fourth, with Hamilton a further two tenths behind in fifth.

"FP1 felt really strong, continuous laps, I thought we were doing pretty well," said Hamilton. "And then FP2, for some reason, the others just took another step. And it’s trying to understand... We didn’t really change anything on the car, but the others took a step somehow.

"These tyres are really, really difficult to get to work. You do an out lap and a prep lap, and they still are not in the window, or they still don’t provide you with the grip. And when you do an extra lap, all of a sudden they switch on, and all of a sudden you have tons more grip.

"So that’s a really fine line and really difficult to get working. We’re trying our best, and some teams do it better than others. So we’ve got to look into that. I think that’s part of it.

"And then our straight-line speed is not as good as Mercedes. Whether or not we can close that deficit tomorrow is what I will try and work on tonight."

Despite looking like Mercedes' closest challenger at times this season, Ferrari have failed to match the German manufacturer of late, falling behind McLaren in the general pecking order.

With its long straights but slow corners, the Baku circuit offers a unique challenge on the F1 calendar, with Ferrari Team Principal Fred Vasseur aware of how Ferrari have struggled at the venue in the past.

"It’s difficult to read. Honestly, the McLaren was very quick, but they didn’t finish the lap. You will need to have a good slipstream, and not to be impeded during the middle part [of the lap]," he said.

"It’s difficult, Baku, [as] we know. If you have a look at last year, we were in a very good shape and we finished 10th and 11th, I think, in Qualifying. Let’s be focused on what we have to do and try to extract the best."

title: Cadillac recruit technical leaders from Red Bull and Ferrari
excerpt:
Cadillac have announced several changes to their technical leadership to be implemented over the coming months, with three figures set to join from rival teams such as Red Bull, Ferrari and Mercedes.

Having made their debut as a Formula 1 team this season, Cadillac have focused on building a robust foundation that they hope will enable them to make progress towards fighting at the front as their experience grows.

As part of that ambition, they have already made a major switch in replacing Graeme Lowdon with Marcin Budkowski in the Team Principal role, owing to his previous stints at multiple championship-winning teams.

Their latest senior appointments see them welcome Craig Skinner as Chief Development Engineer, Eric Blandin as Head of Aerodynamics, and Tim Lean as Chief Engineer – Aerodynamics Modelling and Simulation.

Skinner spent 20 years with Red Bull as their Chief Designer, contributing to their back-to-back titles between 2021 and 2024, and will support the connection between concept, design, analysis and delivery at Cadillac.

Furthermore, Cadillac’s aerodynamics group will be led by Blandin, who has worked in F1 for over 11 years with Mercedes and Aston Martin as Chief Aerodynamicist and Deputy Technical Director respectively.

Rounding out the new technical leadership team will be former McLaren and Red Bull employee Lean. He will also use the expertise gleaned from his five years as principal aerodynamicist at Ferrari to manage Aerodynamics Modelling and Simulation at Cadillac.

An official team statement read: “The Cadillac Formula 1 Team today announced three senior technical appointments that mark an important milestone in the continued technical evolution of the organisation, strengthening leadership across vehicle development and the broader aerodynamics function.

“These key appointments underscore Cadillac Formula 1 Team’s commitment to developing the technical depth, collaboration and accountability required to support its long-term ambitions in Formula 1. They will all join the team in the next few months.”

“These appointments represent a vital step in the technical evolution of the team,” added Budkowski. “Bringing together experienced leadership across development, aerodynamics and modelling will help us create a stronger integrated technical organization and improve performance on track.

"Craig, Eric and Tim bring race and championship-winning experience to Cadillac F1 in areas that are central to our long-term development.”

title: Hadjar encouraged by first day back in his upgraded Red Bull
excerpt:
Isack Hadjar smiled that his Red Bull car felt “better than when I left it” at July’s Hungarian Grand Prix after returning to action during Thursday practice around the Baku City Circuit.

Hadjar missed events at Zandvoort, Monza and the all-new Madring track over the last month, having injured his wrist while training in the summer break.

However, he was finally able to get back into the cockpit of his RB22 in Azerbaijan, where Red Bull have introduced a host of updates – including to the floor body, diffuser and sidepods.

While he lost valuable track time in FP1 due to a gearbox issue, Hadjar got a healthy number of laps under his belt through FP2, which he finished in ninth position, 1.5 seconds away from pace-setter George Russell, and seven tenths behind team mate Max Verstappen.

Summing up his return to action, and how he felt out on track, Hadjar said: “It feels good. It’s been a minute, so it was good. I had a good feeling. Not many laps, unfortunately, today, but this will come. I’m not really worried too much about the pace.

“The feeling… With this new package, we know the characteristic is the same, of the car, but it feels nice. It’s better than when I left it in Budapest, so I’m pretty happy!”

He continued: “I think the car in FP1 was pretty strong. I had like three laps, so I wanted a few changes on the car. They didn’t do what I wanted them to do, so at least we have one clear lead. I’m excited for tomorrow.”

Also speaking to the media post-session, Red Bull Technical Director Pierre Wache offered some more insight into the team’s upgrades and how the pecking order appears to be shaping up this weekend.

“It was quite positive,” Wache said of Red Bull’s day. “Both cars had the upgrade, and that is quite a good sign for us, to be able to produce and to deliver on track this upgrade. From the first analysis in FP1, and I’m waiting on the FP2 one, we more or less delivered what we expected.”

Wache added: “Clearly, Mercedes are in front of us after today, especially on the short runs. I think we have to look at the long runs also, but they look quicker.

“McLaren looks a little bit quicker, or similar to us. After Ferrari it’s difficult to say, because so many people stopped their [soft tyre] lap before the end of the straight, and how you use the energy could be misleading completely the overall lap time.”

Hadjar heads into Friday and Saturday’s running boosted by the news that he will be continuing as Verstappen’s team mate for the 2027 season – Red Bull having activated their option to retain him.

title: Kimi Antonelli hails Baku recovery after unusual encouragement
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli was buoyed by his strong recovery during FP2 at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, having missed a considerable amount of the early running in Baku.

A hydraulics failure almost halfway through FP1, in which he finished fifth-fastest, curtailed his efforts. And there was more inconvenience to come.

"No, actually, I wanted them to spray a bit more because the car caught a bit on fire," Antonelli added.

"Luckily, it didn't do much damage. I was just encouraging them to go [for it]. But yeah, they did what they could."

title: Formula E to race full F1 Mexico City layout as Gen4 arrives
excerpt:
Formula E will use the complete Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez circuit for the Mexico City E-Prix, adopting the same layout used by Formula 1 rather than the shortened track the series has raced on previously.

The revised layout was published after tickets went on general sale for the event, which forms round three of the 2026/27 season, scheduled for 16 January 2027.

The change marks a significant departure from Formula E's previous Mexico City configuration, a roughly 2.6-kilometre track that cut into the infield early and looped back out of the Foro Sol stadium section before rejoining the circuit.

The new layout stretches to the full 4.3-kilometre Grand Prix distance, running the entire length of the main straight, through the sweeping middle Esses, and directly through the stadium section before exiting onto the final part of the Peraltada corner.

While the full layout will be used, tickets have only been released for the Foro Sol stadium, the final corner and the start/finish straight.

One Formula E twist remains as Mexico City modification added

Crucially, the series will tackle the Foro Sol stadium section in identical fashion to F1, sending cars through the tight, technical sequence carved into the old baseball venue.

The section is notoriously demanding even for F1 cars, with Mexico City's 2,200-metre altitude reducing aerodynamic downforce and leaving cars prone to sliding through the slow direction changes inside the stadium.

One addition for the E-Prix will be a chicane on the start-finish straight, inserted to create a dedicated heavy braking zone for energy regeneration.

This chicane will sit at the point where the circuit used to cut into the infield in previous years.

The switch to a full permanent circuit layout is tied directly to Gen4, Formula E's new fourth-generation car making its debut this season.

The car brings 450 kW of race power, a 600 kW attack mode peak, permanent all-wheel drive, and a larger 55 kWh battery, changes that reportedly demand longer, faster circuits capable of sustaining higher energy recovery over extended lap distances.

It is expected that the full Brands Hatch Grand Prix circuit will also be used for its first time hosting Formula E in May next year, while the full Zandvoort layout will not be used.

Based on titles used in recent social media activity by Formula E, these events will likely be known as the British E-Prix and the Dutch E-Prix, in another uncommon move by the championship.

title: Liam Lawson heralded upon much-desired Racing Bulls return
excerpt:
Racing Bulls team principal Alan Permane has praised Liam Lawson after the New Zealander returned to the team.

Lawson was back in the VCARB 03 for the first time since a three-round spell deputising for the injured Isack Hadjar at Red Bull, and immediately went seventh-quickest in Free Practice 1 at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix. The New Zealander, however, dropped to 12th in FP2.

Permane said the 24-year-old had been keen to return to what he described as his own car and believes he has resumed where he left off.

"Very much so," the Racing Bulls boss told Sky Sports F1 when it was put to him how well Lawson performed at Red Bull.

"He enjoyed his time there. He was very much wanting to get back in his car, as he called it: 'I want to be back in my car.' And he's started where he left off, basically; it looks like."

Lawson has scored 45 points across 11 Racing Bulls starts this season, including a career-best fifth in Monaco, helping the team sit fifth in the constructors' standings.

His temporary Red Bull spell, during which he collected 14 points and qualified within a tenth of Max Verstappen at Zandvoort, further strengthened his standing.

A 'very credible job' alongside Verstappen at Red Bull

Hadjar fractured his wrist in a training incident during the summer break, ruling him out of the Dutch, Italian and Spanish Grands Prix.

Lawson was selected to step up and recorded seventh at Zandvoort, sixth in Madrid and P14 at Monza, where his race was compromised by contact with Nico Hulkenberg and a grid penalty.

It marked a contrast to his difficult two-race Red Bull stint at the start of 2025, when he failed to score before being sent back to the junior team.

"I'm super happy for him," Permane added. "Of course, he did a very credible job there. I think we saw in that very first session in Zandvoort, that first qualifying session, he was about a tenth off Max, so that will have boosted his confidence.

"He's certainly come back here [to Racing Bulls] with his head held high and ready to go. But I think it's good for both of them [and Arvid Lindblad].

"They work very, very well together, and certainly we can see that Arvid will be quicker in some corners, Liam will be quicker in others, and throughout the weekend they lift each other up."

Permane also highlighted the progress Lawson has made since returning to Racing Bulls ahead of the 2025 Japanese Grand Prix.

After the setback of his early Red Bull demotion, Lawson rebuilt his form, finishing P14 in last year's championship with 38 points, and — in 2026 — Permane believes that development has continued.

"This year, he's worked very hard; we've worked very hard together, and there's no doubt he's much more focused," he said of Lawson since he returned to the team for the first time ahead of the Japanese Grand Prix last season.

"He's driving better. He's better on track, off track. I think in all areas he's better, and that's down to his hard work."

title: Lewis Hamilton confirms driver talks after scary near-miss
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has confirmed he will raise a scary closing-speed incident involving Liam Lawson with fellow drivers at the next briefing, after the pair were involved in a near-miss during second practice for the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

The Ferrari driver was on a slow lap approaching the final sector at Baku when Lawson, driving for Racing Bulls, closed up on him dramatically faster than expected as he began his own flying lap.

Hamilton said he believed he had left sufficient margin before the incident occurred, but the gap evaporated once his Ferrari's power dropped off entering Turn 18. The moment saw the veteran receive a reprimand, following a stewards investigation.

Hamilton finished fifth in second practice, with George Russell topping the times ahead of team-mate Kimi Antonelli and Max Verstappen. Lawson ended the session down in 12th.

Asked whether he was concerned about closing speeds in qualifying following the incident, Hamilton told reporters after the session that the topic will be discussed by the drivers.

"Yeah, we debated it, and I'm sure we're going to talk about it in the drivers' briefing," he said.

"Basically, with the rules that the FIA gave us this year, when you come into the weekend, there's no data or simulations to say, okay, when you come to the last corner and you go to full throttle and you have 500 brake horsepower less than the car behind you on the lap, this is the gap you need to have before they get on your [rear]."

"They don't tell you the closing speed that you're going to have, and I was four seconds ahead basically. I went into the last corner pushing. I could see him, but I thought the gap was enough. I got into full throttle, and then literally as we got into Turn 18, it's like the car just died, and he swamped up the gap massively."

"And that could happen to anyone. So I think it's having clearer guidelines from them, because none of the drivers want to get in trouble. None of them are trying to get in the way of anybody."

Lewis Hamilton proposes guidelines solution

Hamilton has already put forward a possible solution to the FIA, aimed at removing the huge power differential between cars on push laps and those cruising through the final sector.

His suggestion centres on Turns 18 and 19, the final corners before the pit straight at Baku, where the disparity between a car deploying full hybrid power and one conserving energy on an out-lap or slow lap becomes most dangerous.

"Like, that's our sole goal, is to get out the way and then also get our lap, and so I think we'll talk about in the drivers' briefing about what we could do," Hamilton added.

"I mean, I said to them what they should do is, on a single lap, when we're doing a push lap, we get max power out the last corner. When you come through Turn 19, it resets, and then you have more power, a little bit more power in there."

"And there should just be nobody going slow ever through Turns 18 and 19. So you should just, even if you're on a slow lap, still have to go flat out through Turns 18 and 19 with full power, and that would mean that no one's ever going slow through that section."

"I think that's something we'll talk about."

title: Mercedes leave F1 rivals facing awkward questions after dominant Baku display
excerpt:
Does anyone have an answer to Mercedes pace?

Mercedes emerged as the outright pace-setter through both practice sessions for the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, with George Russell topping both FP1 and FP2 at the Baku City Circuit.

Russell's one minute 43.347s in the second session was over eight-tenths clear of the closest Red Bull, a gap far too large to be explained by fuel loads or engine modes alone.

Team-mate Kimi Antonelli backed that pace up with second place in FP2, giving Mercedes a striking one-two on a track where straight-line efficiency has historically mattered more than almost anywhere else on the calendar.

That straight-line strength appears to be central to the Brackley-based squad's advantage. With Baku's 2.2-kilometre back straight rewarding low-drag efficiency, and neither Mercedes nor Ferrari submitting any new aerodynamic components for this weekend, the W17's edge is a case of underlying car performance rather than a fresh upgrade unlocking lap time.

Red Bull, by contrast, arrived with five separate updates, including revised floor and diffuser geometries, modified split lines to the floor and new cooling louvres aimed at reliability.

The team has confirmed the changes represent its final major development step of the 2026 campaign. Max Verstappen showed encouraging pace across both sessions, second in FP1 and third in FP2, but still finished 0.827s off Russell's benchmark in the afternoon running, suggesting the new parts have yet to close the gap to Mercedes.

[Article continues below]

© XPBimages

Ferrari's low-key approach

Ferrari took a notably different route, bringing no updates at all and instead concentrating its practice programme on qualifying preparation.

Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton finished third and fourth in FP1 before slipping to fourth and fifth in FP2, with the team seemingly wrestling with tyre warm-up over single flying laps.

Ferrari's practice pace lagged not just behind Mercedes but Red Bull, too, across both sessions. Whether that gap reflects genuine underlying deficit or simply Ferrari's stated focus on race-simulation work rather than low-fuel heroics remains an open question heading into qualifying.

[Article continues below]

© XPBimages

McLaren disrupted by floor issues

McLaren's day was complicated by teething problems with an extensive eight-part upgrade package, covering revised sidepod inlets, engine cover, floor edges, diffuser layout, rear suspension fairings and the reintroduction of the team's H-wing.

Floorboard attachment issues disrupted the Woking-based squad's practice programme, and the on-track results reflected that turbulence.

Oscar Piastri was McLaren's stronger performer in FP1, sixth quickest, before dropping to eighth in FP2 as Lando Norris improved from 14th to sixth across the two sessions.

The scale of the update suggests McLaren is targeting a meaningful step in both low-speed traction through Baku's castle section and high-speed stability on the straights, but the makeshift repairs mean it remains unclear how representative the day's times were of the package's true potential.

[Article continues below]

Brakes and grip define the challenge

Beyond the upgrade battle, the day's running underlined the physical demands of Baku's unique layout. Heavy braking zones into Turn 1 and Turn 3, combined with low track grip typical of a street circuit early in a race weekend, produced reports of front locking and brake balance trouble across the field.

That combination, low-drag efficiency on the straight paired against mechanical grip through the slow corners, remains the defining aerodynamic compromise of this circuit, and it appears to be one Mercedes has currently solved better than anyone.

With Friday qualifying to follow, after the schedule was moved forward by a day to accommodate Azerbaijan's National Day of Remembrance, Mercedes will start as clear favourites on raw pace.

But Red Bull's final development push, Ferrari's qualifying-focused conservatism and McLaren's unresolved floor troubles all leave genuine uncertainty over how the order will settle once the sessions begin that actually count.

title: Lewis Hamilton learns stewards verdict after 'dangerous' Liam Lawson incident
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has been handed a reprimand by Azerbaijan Grand Prix stewards following his "f****** dangerous" impeding of Liam Lawson in practice.

During FP2, with Lawson on a flying lap, Hamilton moved slowly through Turn 19, the final, unsighted corner on the lap as cars thread the needle between the barriers.

Lawson was unimpressed over the radio, branding the move "f****** dangerous" as he was forced to check up and avoid ramming into the back of the Ferrari.

Ultimately, the stewards decided to hand Hamilton a reprimand, his second of the season.

It was found during the investigation that Hamilton had failed to follow the race director's competition notes, ordering cars on out or slow laps to "remain on the extreme left from the exit of Turn 16 to the entry of Turn 18" so they can then avoid impeding into Turn 19.

Hamilton did not remain on the extreme left and stayed on the racing line as Lawson approached, causing the lift-off, and Hamilton did not follow the race director's instructions, and therefore "unnecessarily impeded" Lawson.

With the "severe" nature of the impeding, the reprimand was issued, although the stewards did take into account the "difficulty to manage energy deployment from Turn 16 to Turn 19 and the end of the lap."

title: Lando Norris suffering 'knife in the heart' over McLaren Baku reality
excerpt:
Lando Norris says seeing how far McLaren is off the pace compared to Mercedes in Azerbaijan is like "a little knife in the heart."

The MCL40 has received upgrades in Baku, but Norris, the lead McLaren in FP2, was 1.484s slower than George Russell's un-upgraded Mercedes.

The Baku City Circuit was not expected to favour McLaren, with its slow-speed corners exposing a long-held weakness in the chassis, whilst the longest straight on the calendar means the draggy nature of the machine is being shown.

Furthermore, McLaren had a tricky day with the new upgrades, especially in FP1, where both Norris and team-mate Oscar Piastri lost time whilst checks were made throughout the session.

Whilst he felt that the car was "not that bad", Norris spoke of the "pretty pants" feeling he had experienced.

"We're miles off, I mean we're up there, and in a position we expect to be in, but like 1.5s off the pace is pretty pants," Norris explained.

"We'll see what work we can do [overnight], and the car doesn't feel that bad; it is just a little knife in the heart when you see how far off you are.

"I don't really care how confident I am in the car; I just care about the pace, and we're not very fast, so I don't care.

"I drive whatever car I am given, and I just want it to be quick, and it's not very quick at the moment, but we will see what we can change."

The article continues below.

Norris reflects on tough McLaren day

Further reflecting on the tough day, Norris explained how the track layout was not helping the MCL40.

"It was a tricky start after losing some laps in FP1, which wasn’t ideal, but the team in the garage did a solid job to get the cars ready for FP2, and that’s a positive we’ll carry forward," he said.

"Overall, the car actually feels pretty good to drive, but on a slow-speed track with a long straight, we’re losing out and being off the pace is a tough start.

"We’ll now dig into the data overnight and see what we can change for [Friday's] sessions, I hope we can close some of the gap.

"We’ll keep our heads down and try to maximise what we have for the remainder of the weekend."

title: Cadillac boost F1 team with major former Red Bull, Mercedes signings
excerpt:
Cadillac has announced the triple signings of Craig Skinner, Eric Blandin, and Tim Lean to boost its F1 technical team.

F1's newest team has already undergone a major transformation with a change in team principal during its debut season with Marcin Budkowski replacing Graeme Lowdon during the summer break, with the team now securing the services of world championship and race-winning expertise in the form of Skinner, Blandin and Lean.

Skinner joins as chief development engineer, whilst Blandin is head of aerodynamics.

Lean is the new chief engineer - aerodynamics modeling and simulation.

Skinner (below) was most previously the chief designer at Red Bull, serving in the position since 2022 until earlier this year, and was responsible for assisting in the development of some of F1's most successful cars.

He was chief designer for the RB19 of 2023 which won 21 of 22 races and is statistically, the most successful F1 car of all-time as Max Verstappen crushed the opposition on his way to a third drivers' title.

Blandin has worked for Red Bull, Ferrari, Mercedes, and Aston Martin during a long career in F1, alongside drivers such as Fernando Alonso, Lewis Hamilton and Nico Rosberg, and was Mercedes' chief aerodynamicist from 2017, when the team aced the new technical regulations, culminating in the W11 of 2020.

Lean is an engineering consultant with decades of experience, including at McLaren, Red Bull, and Ferrari. He was most recently head of aerodynamic innovation at Ferrari, leaving in 2022 before setting up his own engineering consultantcy.

He was also a senior aerodynamicist at Airbus and was responsible for transonic wing design.

The article continues below.

Cadillac shakes up technical team with new signings

Reflecting, Budkowski called the signings a "vital step in the technical evolution of the team."

"Bringing together experienced leadership across development, aerodynamics and modelling will help us create a stronger integrated technical organization and improve performance on track," he said.

"Craig, Eric and Tim bring race and championship-winning experience to Cadillac F1 in areas that are central to our long-term development."

title: F1 bosses to hold FIA talks over revolutionary rule change
excerpt:
The framework of the new engine regulations continues to be discussed by teams, power unit manufacturers, and the FIA.

24 September 4:30PM

Audi boss Mattia Binotto has confirmed that an IndyCar-style 'Push to Pass' system is being discussed as the new engine regulations take shape.

F1 is set to return to V8 engines by the start of the next decade, either in 2030 or 2031, with discussions taking place between teams, power unit manufacturers, and the FIA to design the rules, with the 2026 rules first being unveiled in 2022.

Grand prix racing will abandon the turbo hybrid units, although there is some discussion over whether electrical elements should remain in the new engines, and to what extent.

In 2026, drivers are armed with 'overtake' and 'boost' modes, with overtake replacing the old DRS, whilst 'boost' deploys more power, although drivers cannot currently manage the deployment of energy themselves, with it being controlled through on-board computer algorithms.

As the discussions continue for the framework of the post-2029 rules, Audi chief Binotto confirmed that a 'Push to Pass' style overtaking aid is being considered, with F1 previously using a version of this with KERS between 2009 and 2013.

"Yes, it is on the menu," Binotto confirmed when asked by media, including RacingNews365, if push to pass would feature in discussions over the shape of the future engine regulations.

"Push to pass is important for the racing situation, for overtaking, and making sure that we are not creating trains and no one can overtake.

"So a push-to-pass will be there. What type of push-to-pass is still to be discussed.

"So there is not a clear way of doing it; there are multiple ways of doing it.

"It can be boost pressure, it can be DRS, it can be KERS, so electrical, so the way we will do it will be part of the discussions with the FIA."

The article continues below.

© XPBimages

Binotto declares Audi stance

Binotto then went into detail as he discussed Audi's stance on what the V8 regulations would look like.

The team was enticed into grand prix racing for the first time by the 2026 rules, and spent heavily to design the current iteration of the V6 turbo hybrids, which will be consigned to history.

Binotto signalled that Audi would be in favour of the change to V8 equipment.

"There is no clarity yet, so we know that the FIA is still elaborating on what maybe the concepts they would like to propose," said Binotto.

"We know it's a V8 for 2030 at the earliest, but the timing is uncertain.

"Development has to start before the end of the year. I think the regulation needs to be agreed and voted on before the end of the year to have certainty and clarity on by 2027 to start the design and concept phase.

"What's the main objective we are looking at? I think we are we all agree. First, there will be significant cost savings required. The current power unit is still very expensive, and we believe that having a clear target on cost would be important when considering the format of the V8 itself.

"We believe that we still need to retain some advanced technologies. I think that F1 has always been the edge of a platform for innovation ahead of technology, and we believe whatever will be the overall format, it has to remain a platform for innovation for all the manufacturers.

"So yes, we welcome the V8, welcome a better sound, we welcome cost saving, but when it comes to the details of hybrid, I would say yes, turbo, possibly yes, but all the details, I think exactly need to be discussed with the FIA.

"That's why I think that discussion will start very soon. As Audi, we are very open, very collaborative, and I'm pretty sure that together with the FIA, we will find the right compromise."

title: Jamie Chadwick makes F1 debut in important Williams test
excerpt:
Jamie Chadwick has sampled Formula 1 machinery for the first time in a recent TPC test with the Williams team.

The three-time W Series champion drove the 2025 FW47 machine in a test at Portimao in Portugal on Monday 21st September, totalling 32 laps as she became the first British woman since Jessica Hawkins in 2023 to drive an F1 machine.

The last woman to drive an F1 car was Mercedes' Doriane Pin in the 2021 Mercedes earlier this year.

Chadwick, who serves as Williams' F1 Academy advisor to the team's Jade Jacquet, became the first woman to win an Indy NXT race in 2024, at Road America, and is currently competing in the European Le Mans Series.

The Briton is the first woman to drive an F1 Williams since Susie Wolff in 2015, when she competed in multiple FP1 sessions, where, in 2014, she became the first woman in over two decades to drive a grand prix car.

The test served importance for Williams as it gathered data ahead of F1's return to Portugal in 2027.

"It was a phenomenal day and an incredible experience. Few things can prepare you for driving a Formula 1 car at speed around a track like Portimão, but it was everything I imagined and 10 times more," said Chadwick, who drove the car Carlos Sainz guided to two grand prix podiums and a Sprint third.

"I’m incredibly grateful to the Williams F1 Team for this opportunity. I remember being young and watching Susie Wolff step into a Williams F1 car and how much that inspired my own journey.

"I’d love to be able to do the same for the next generation, and the experience I gained today will make a real difference both to my own racing and to what I can pass on to the drivers coming through. I’m so grateful and incredibly happy with how the day went.

"It’s an experience I’ll remember for a very long time - I’d go as far as saying it’s been the best day of my life so far."

Reflecting, Williams boss James Vowles called Chadwick an "inspiration to millions."

"Jamie Chadwick is an inspiration for millions of women and girls who have broken records at every level, and she has thoroughly earned this F1 test opportunity with the Williams F1 Team," he said.

"Jamie gathered important data for the team as F1 prepares to return to Portimão next year, and her feedback and performance were impressive as we knew they would be.

"This clearly shows there is a path for women to compete at the top level, and I look forward to seeing how Jamie uses this experience to advance her own driving and advise our young drivers on what it takes to drive an F1 car."

title: George Russell sets personal F1 season first as Arvid Lindblad crashes again
excerpt:
George Russell remarkably became only the second driver this season to top the opening two practice sessions of a grand prix weekend.

A significant tow along the main straight at the Baku City Circuit enabled Russell to comfortably beat Red Bull's Max Verstappen by four-tenths of a second in FP1.

In FP2, Russell finished just over half a second clear of Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli, who missed most of the first session and 30 minutes of the second following a hydraulics failure on his W17 in FP1 that necessitated a power unit change in between.

Only Antonelli had previously finished quickest in FP1 and FP2 this season, doing so ahead of the Austrian GP.

Russell posted a lap of one minute 43.347s to spearhead a comfortable Mercedes one-two, with Verstappen over eight-tenths of a second adrift to sit third on the timesheet, followed by Ferrari duo Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton.

The seven-time F1 champion is under investigation by the stewards, however, for seriously impeding Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson.

[Article continues below]

On his return to Red Bull, after missing the last three grands prix due to a wrist injury sustained during the summer break, Isac Hadjar was the first driver to venture onto the soft tyres, producing a lap of 1:45.462s, just under a second behind Verstappen.

After 20 minutes, Arvid Lindblad sparked the first red flag of the event, clipping a barrier hard with the right-rear of his Racing Bulls on the approach into the castle section. There was a secondary impact with a barrier 20 metres later before he eventually came to a rest further up the hill.

It was Lindblad's second successive FP2 crash after doing so in the Spanish GP in Madrid 13 days ago.

Following a nine-minute delay to clear the debris, the remainder of the field filed out on soft rubber given the time lost, embarking on their first serious push laps of the day.

For Haas driver Oliver Bearman, however, the rest of his session lasted no more than a few seconds as his car switched off between Turns 1 and 2. The Briton radioed in to say his "engine broke".

On his first flying lap since retiring in FP1, Antonelli managed to post the sixth-quickest lap at that stage.

Team-mate Russell then set the benchmark with a lap of 1:43.759s, and although Verstappen purpled the first sector soon after, he finished four-tenths of a second adrift by its culmination.

McLaren's Lando Norris then appeared as if he would go quickest after beating Verstappen's first sector time, and with the benefit of a tow along the main straight from Audi's Nico Hulkenberg, only to abort the lap.

Russell, though, improved on his leading time by four-tenths of a second to become the first driver to dip below one minute 44 seconds, to comfortably take the honours.

Norris finished sixth quickest ahead of Alpine's Pierre Gasly, followed by the second McLaren of Oscar Piastri. Hadjar and Haas' Esteban Ocon completed the top 10.
